doc.title: Bill Allred interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 24, 2017

title: Few African American players and audiences
summary: Allred discusses why few black musicians appear at trad jazz parties and a request for a black Dixieland band.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Why is it that there seems to be very few African American people in the audience, and sometimes on the bandstand, depending on the style of music.

Yeah. And there are a few. I guess it’s the Uncle Tom thing. A lot of them just associate that music with the old days when Teddy Wilson couldn’t find a hotel because he was black or something like that. And I don’t know who’s — I guess family-wise and friend- wise they’re cultivating that. They’re keeping that going faster than we’re getting them to play in parties and groups you know. I had a call — in my career in Orlando, which is kind of waning, I mean there’s not much going on, you know I used to book some things and people would call me up and say, “Yeah I need this group.” The guy wanted a black Dixieland band for this party. I said, “We don’t have anyone.” I mean there’s a band with a couple of black guys in it. Like in my 8-piece band I have a trumpet player who’s mother’s black and his dad’s Hispanic. That’s as close as we can come. But there are, the people like the black trumpet players, there’s three or four of them, they all did the Louis time on the shows and then the black trombone player — my son even recorded an album with.

Wycliffe. So there are those. And I remember I was with Wild Bill Davison’s, I mean I never played with so many hotshot musicians in my life as the old Norway ship jazz parties with Hank and Shelly used to book the musicians.
